text: Practice problem 2 November 29, 2025 Problem 1. Let A, B, C, D ∈ Mn×n(F ) (i.e. every pair among A, B, C, D commutes). Show that the determinant of the 2n × 2n block matrix (A B C D ) equals det(AD − BC). Problem 2. Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ), A ̸= 0. If r is any integer with 1 ≤ r ≤ n, an r × r submatrix of A means any matrix obtained from A by deleting (n − r) rows and (n − r) columns. The determinant rank of A is defined to be the largest positive integer r for which some r × r submatrix of A has nonzero determinant. Prove that the determinant rank of A equals the rank of A. Problem 3. Let B ∈ Mn×n(F ) be fixed. Define linear operators TB : Mn×n(F ) → Mn×n(F ) by TB(A) = AB. (i) Show that det(TB) = (det B)n. (ii) Show that the minimal polynomial of the linear operator TB equals the minimal polynomial of the matrix B. Problem 4. Let A, B ∈ Mn×n(F ). Show that if A is invertible then there are at most n scalars c ∈ F for which the matrix cA + B is not invertible. Problem 5. Let A ∈ Mn×n(R) satisfy A2 = I. (i) Show that A is invertible and det(A) = ±1. (ii) Show that the eigenvalues of A are 1 and −1. (iii) Show that A is diagonalizable over R. (iv) Let m+ and m− be the multiplicities of 1 and −1 as eigenvalues. Show that m+ + m− = n and det(A) = (−1)m−. (v) Compute tr(A) in terms of m+ and m−. (vi) Find the characteristic polynomial pA(x) of A. Problem 6. Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ) be nilpotent: i.e. Am = 0 and Am−1 ̸= 0 for some m ≥ 1. (i) Show that m ≤ n. (ii) Find pA(x). 1 (iii) Show that det(I − A) = 1. (iv) Show that tr(A) = 0. (v) dim ker N k > dim ker N k−1 for any 1 ≤ k ≤ m. (vi) If m = n ≥ 2, show that there is no A ∈ Mn×n(F ) such that A2 = N . Hint for (v): Consider v such that N m−1v ̸= 0. For which l is N m−kv ∈ ker N l? Hint for (vi): What is the minimal polynomial of A? Problem 7. If A ∈ Mn×n(R) satisfies det(A) < 0, then A has at least one real eigen- value. Problem 8. Let A ∈ Mn×n(R). If n = 2m + 1 is odd, then A has a real eigenvalue. Problem 9. Let A ∈ M2×2(F ). Show that A = D + N where D is diagonalizable, N is nilpotent and DN = N D. Problem 10. Let A ∈ Mn×n(C) be invertible. Show that if Am is diagonalizable for some positive integer m, then A is also diagonalizable. Hint: If λ ̸= 0 then there are m distinct solutions to xm = λ in C. Problem 11. Let A := (2 0 2 3 ) and define the map T : M2×2(R) → M2×2(R) by T (B) = AB − BA. (i) Show that the identity matrix I ∈ M2×2(R) and A are in ker T . (ii) Choose a basis β of M2×2(R) and compute [T ] β β. (iii) Give all eigenvalues of T . (iv) Give a basis of the eigenspace corresponding to the eigenvalue 0. (v) Give the characteristic and the minimal polynomials, and the Jordan form of T . Is T diagonalizable? Problem 12. (i) Let A, B ∈ Mn×n(C). Show that pA(B) is invertible if and only if A, B have no common eigenvalue. (ii) Let A, B, C ∈ Mn×n(C) be such that AC = CB. Show that for any f (x) ∈ F [x], we have f (A)X = Xf (B). (iii) Let A, B, C ∈ Mn×n(C) be such that AC = CB. Suppose A, B have no common eigenvalue, show that C = 0. Problem 13. Let A ∈ Mm×n(F ) and B ∈ Mn×m(F ). Show that tr(AB) = tr(BA). Problem 14. (i) Let A ∈ Mm×n(F ) and B ∈ Mn×m(F ). Prove that all non-zero eigen- values of AB are also eigenvalues of BA, and show how the corresponding eigenvectors are related. (ii) Prove that the prior statement extends to zero eigenvalues when A, B ∈ Mn×n(F ): if AB has zero as an eigenvalue, so does BA. (iii) Does the extension of part (ii) to zero eigenvalues hold when A and B are more general rectangular matrices, as in part (i)? Prove it or provide a counterexample. 2 Problem 15. (i) Let A, B ∈ Mn×n(F ). Prove that if I − AB is invertible then I − BA is invertible and (I − BA)−1 = I + B(I − AB) −1A. (ii) Use the (i) to prove that, if A, B ∈ Mn×n(F ), then the AB and BA have precisely the same eigenvalues in F (counted with algebraic multiplicity). (iii) Do AB and BA necessarily have the same minimal polynomial? Problem 16. Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ) and let V1, V2 ⊂ F n be subspaces satisfying A(V1) ⊂ V1, A(V2) ⊂ V2 and F n = V1 ⊕ V2 Prove that A is similar to a block diagonal matrix (B 0 0 C ) , where B is an r × r matrix and C is an (n − r) × (n − r) matrix for r = dim V1. Problem 17. Let A be an n×n real matrix with distinct (possibly complex) eigenvalues λ1, . . . , λn, and corresponding eigenvectors v1, . . . , vn. Assume that λ1 = 1 and that |λj| < 1 for 2 ≤ j ≤ n. (i) Prove that limp→∞ Apv exists for any v ∈ Cn. (ii) Define T : Cn → Cn by T (v) = lim p→∞ Apv. Find the dimensions of the kernel and image of T and give bases for both. Problem 18. Let A be a 3 × 3 real matrix satisfying the equation 16A3 = 24A 2 − 7A − I. (i) Show that the sequence Ak converges as k → ∞. (ii) Let B be the matrix limit of the sequence Ak. Show that B2 = B. Problem 19. Let A = 1 2 (−1 2 −1 1 ) , and f (x) = 1 1 − x = 1 + x + x 2 + · · · = ∞∑ k=0 xk. (i) Find an invertible matrix P such that P −1AP = D is a diagonal matrix. (ii) Find f (A). (iii) Verify that f (A)(I − A) = I. 3 Problem 20. Suppose (zn) is a sequence of complex numbers (not all zero) that satisfy zn+1 = zn + 1 4 zn−1. (i) Show that if z0 = 0 and z1 = 1, then zn+1 zn → r as n → ∞. Identify r. (ii) Find numbers a and b so that |zn| → 0 as n → ∞ if and only if az1 + bz0 = 0. Problem 21. In 1970 there were 2 flowers in Wonderland. The next year there were 14 flowers. Then each subsequent year there were exactly twice as many flowers as in the previous year plus three times as many flowers as in the year before the previous one. How many flowers were there in Wonderland in 2021? Problem 22. The populations of deer and wolves in Yellowstone are well approximated by the recurrence relations: dn+1 = 5 4 dn − 1 4 wn, wn+1 = 1 4 dn + 3 4 wn, where dn and wn denote the number of deer and wolves, respectively, in year n, for n = 0, 1, 2, . . .. Assuming that initially there are more deer than wolves (i.e., w0 < d0), what is the proportion between the number of deer and wolves as n → ∞? That is, compute: lim n→∞ dn wn . Problem 23. The Fibonacci sequence F0, F1, F2, . . . is defined by F0 = 0, F1 = 1, Fn = Fn−2 + Fn−1 for n ≥ 2. Define A = (0 1 1 1 ). (i) Show that A ( Fn−2 Fn−1 ) = (Fn−1 Fn ) . Conclude that An ( 0 1 ) = ( Fn Fn+1 ) for each nonnegative integer n. (ii) Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of A. (iii) Use (ii) and (i) to compute An ( 0 1 ) . Conclude that Fn = 1 √5 [( 1 + √5 2 )n − ( 1 − √5 2 )n] for each nonnegative integer n. 4 Problem 24. Let the cyclic shift mapping S acting on vectors x ∈ Cn be defined as: S(x1, x2, . . . , xn) = (x2, . . . , xn, x1). (i) Determine the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of S. Hint: xn = 1 has solutions 1, ζ, · · · , ζ n−1 where ζ = e2πi/n. (ii) Consider the n × n matrices A =        a1 a2 . . . an−1 an an a1 . . . an−2 an−1 ... ... ... ... a3 a4 . . . a1 a2 a2 a3 . . . an a1        Show that the eigenvalues of A are of the form λk+1 = a1 + a2ωk + a3ω2 k + · · · + anω n−1 k , 0 ≤ k ≤ n − 1, where ωk = ζ k. Hint: A = f (S) where f (x) = a1 + a2x + a3x2 + · · · + anx n−1. (iii) Compute the determinant of C =        0 1 1 . . . 1 1 0 1 . . . 1 1 1 0 . . . 1 ... ... ... ... 1 1 . . . 1 0        . (iv) Think of Cn as the space of discrete periodic functions, i.e., identify xn+1 ≡ x1 and x0 ≡ xn. Consider the linear transformations corresponding to the discrete first and second derivatives: (∆x)k = xk+1 − xk, (∆ 2x)k = xk+1 − 2xk + xk−1. Show that both ∆ and ∆2 commute with the cyclic shift operator S, and use this fact to find their eigenvalues and eigenvectors. 5
